scope: One unscored current-selector preflight from previously selected public evidence, not a benchmark or confirmation. No tools or additional production calls.

row.label: Using SQLite’s documentation, explain how to enable foreign-key enforcement for each connection

rows.rendered: | See evidence | Using SQLite’s documentation, explain how to enable foreign-key enforcement for each connection | To get the protection you actually want, run \`PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;\` at the start of every connection: / The pragma is per-connection, not per-database - the setting isn't stored in the file. / Most production code runs \`PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;\` immediately after opening a connection. / - \`foreign_keys=ON\` is unrelated to WAL but worth setting on every connection - SQLite leaves foreign key enforcement off by default for backward compatibility. | [4][5] |

row.label: whether WAL permits a reader alongside a writer

rows.rendered: | True | whether WAL permits a reader alongside a writer | Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of readers, writers and readers can run at the same time. / The result: a writer and any number of readers can be active at the same moment. / What WAL does change is that readers no longer block the writer, and the writer no longer blocks readers. | [1][5] |

row.label: supports a database on a network filesystem.

rows.rendered: | Not true | supports a database on a network filesystem. | The wal-index greatly improves the performance of readers, but the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the same machine. / This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem. / - \*\*Network filesystems.\*\* WAL relies on shared memory (\`mmap\` ) between processes accessing the database. / NFS, SMB, and similar don't support that reliably. | [1][5] |
